In [[Matrix (mathematics)|matrix theory]], the '''Frobenius covariants''' of a [[square matrix]]  {{mvar|A}} are special polynomials of it, namely  [[projection (linear algebra)|projection]]  matrices {{math|''F''<sub>''i''</sub>(''A'')}} associated with the [[eigenvalue, eigenvector and eigenspace|eigenvalues and eigenvectors]] of  {{mvar|A}}.<ref name=horn>Roger A. Horn and Charles R. Johnson (1991), ''Topics in Matrix Analysis''. Cambridge University Press, {{ISBN|978-0-521-46713-1}}</ref>{{rp|pp.403,437–8}} They are named after the mathematician [[Ferdinand Georg Frobenius|Ferdinand Frobenius]].

Each covariant is a [[projection (linear algebra)|projection]]  on the [[eigenvalue, eigenvector and eigenspace|eigenspace]] associated with the eigenvalue ''λ''<sub>''i''</sub>.
Frobenius covariants are the coefficients of [[Sylvester's formula]], which expresses a [[matrix function|function of a matrix]] {{math|''f''(''A'')}} as a [[matrix polynomial]], namely a linear combination 
of that function's  values on the eigenvalues of {{mvar|A}}.

==Formal definition==
Let {{mvar|A}} be a [[diagonalizable matrix]] with eigenvalues ''λ''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''λ''<sub>''k''</sub>.

The Frobenius covariant {{math|''F''<sub>''i''</sub>(''A'')}}, for ''i'' = 1,..., ''k'', is the matrix
:<math> F_i (A) \equiv  \prod_{j=1 \atop j \ne i}^k \frac{1}{\lambda_i-\lambda_j} (A - \lambda_j I)~. </math>
It is essentially the [[Lagrange polynomial]] with matrix argument. If the eigenvalue  ''λ''<sub>''i''</sub> is simple, then as an idempotent projection matrix to a one-dimensional subspace, {{math|''F''<sub>''i''</sub>(''A'')}} has a unit [[Trace (linear algebra)|trace]].

{{see also|Resolvent formalism}}

==Computing the covariants==
[[File:GeorgFrobenius.jpg|180px|thumb|right|[[Ferdinand Georg Frobenius]] (1849–1917), German mathematician. His main interests were [[elliptic function]]s, [[differential equation]]s, and later [[group theory]].]]

The Frobenius covariants of a matrix {{mvar|A}} can be obtained from any [[eigendecomposition]] {{math|''A'' {{=}} ''SDS''<sup>−1</sup>}}, where {{mvar|S}} is non-singular and {{mvar|D}} is diagonal with {{math|''D''<sub>''i'',''i''</sub> {{=}} ''λ''<sub>''i''</sub>}}. 
The matrix {{mvar|S}} is defined up to multiplication on the right by a [[diagonal matrix]].
If {{mvar|A}} has no multiple eigenvalues, then let ''c''<sub>''i''</sub> be the {{mvar|i}}th right eigenvector of {{mvar|A}}, that is, the {{mvar|i}}th column of {{mvar|S}}; and let ''r''<sub>''i''</sub> be the {{mvar|i}}th left eigenvector of {{mvar|A}}, namely the {{mvar|i}}th row of {{mvar|S}}<sup>−1</sup>.  Then {{math|''F''<sub>''i''</sub>(''A'') {{=}} ''c''<sub>''i''</sub> ''r''<sub>''i''</sub>}}. 
As a projection matrix, the Frobenius covariant satisfies the relation
:<math> F_i (A)F_j (A) =  \delta_{ij}F_i (A), </math>
which leads to
{{math| ''r''<sub>''i''</sub> ''c''<sub>''j''</sub> {{=}} δ<sub>''ij''</sub>. }}

Given that  
{{mvar|v}} and {{mvar|w}} are the right and left vectors satisfying 
{{math|''w'' ''F''<sub>''i''</sub>(''A'') ''v'' {{≠}} 0}},
the right and left eigenvectors of {{mvar|A}} may be written as 
{{math|''c''<sub>''i''</sub> {{=}} ''N''<sub>''ci''</sub> ''F''<sub>''i''</sub>(''A'') ''v''}}
and 
{{math|''r''<sub>''i''</sub> {{=}} ''N''<sub>''ri''</sub> ''w'' ''F''<sub>''i''</sub>(''A'')}}. 
The orthonormality of the eigenvectors gives one constraint for the normalization coefficients. The remaining freedom is related to the choice of representation for the matrix {{mvar|S}}. 

If {{mvar|A}} has an eigenvalue ''λ''<sub>''i''</sub> appearing multiple times, then {{math|''F''<sub>''i''</sub>(''A'') {{=}} Σ<sub>''j''</sub> ''c''<sub>''j''</sub> ''r''<sub>''j''</sub>}}, where the sum is over all rows and columns associated with the eigenvalue ''λ''<sub>''i''</sub>.<ref name=horn/>{{rp|p.521}}

==Example==
Consider the two-by-two matrix:
:<math> A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 4 & 2 \end{bmatrix}.</math>
This matrix has two eigenvalues, 5 and −2, which can be found by solving the [[Characteristic polynomial|characteristic equation]]. By virtue of the [[Cayley–Hamilton theorem]], {{math| (''A'' − 5)(''A'' + 2) {{=}} 0}}.

The corresponding eigen decomposition is
:<math> A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1/7 \\ 4 & -1/7 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1/7 \\ 4 & -1/7 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1/7 \\ 4 & -1/7 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1/7 & 1/7 \\ 4 & -3 \end{bmatrix}. </math>
Hence the Frobenius covariants, manifestly projections,  are 
:<math> \begin{array}{rl}
F_1(A) &= c_1 r_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1/7 & 1/7 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3/7 & 3/7 \\ 4/7 & 4/7 \end{bmatrix} = F_1^2(A)\\
F_2(A) &= c_2 r_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1/7 \\ -1/7 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4/7 & -3/7 \\ -4/7 & 3/7 \end{bmatrix}=F_2^2(A) ~,
\end{array} </math>
with
:<math>F_1(A) F_2(A) = 0 , \qquad F_1(A) + F_2(A) = I ~.</math>
Note {{math|tr{{nnbsp}}''F''<sub>1</sub>(''A'') {{=}} tr{{nnbsp}}''F''<sub>2</sub> (''A''){{=}} 1}}, as required.

== Generalization ==
When a square matrix <math display="inline">A \in \mathbb{C}^{n \times n}</math> has repeated eigenvalues (such as a [[defective matrix]] or a diagonalizable one), the standard definition of Frobenius covariants based on Lagrange polynomials becomes undefined due to division by zero.

In this general case, let <math display="inline">\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k</math> be the distinct eigenvalues of {{mvar|A}}, each with an [[algebraic multiplicity]] of <math display="inline">m_i + 1</math>. The generalized Frobenius covariants <math display="inline">A_i \in \mathbb{C}^{n \times n}</math> are projection matrices (<math display="inline">A_i^2 = A_i</math>) that project <math display="inline">\mathbb{C}^n</math> onto the [[generalized eigenspace]] corresponding to <math display="inline">\lambda_i</math> along the [[Direct sum of modules|direct sum]] of the remaining generalized eigenspaces, satisfying <math display="inline">\sum_{i=1}^k A_i = I</math>.

The generalized Frobenius covariants <math display="inline">A_i</math> can be constructed using several equivalent methods.

=== Construction via Hermite interpolation ===
{{See also|Hermite interpolation}}
To generalize the projection matrices for cases with repeated eigenvalues, one can use [[Hermite interpolation|Hermite interpolating polynomials]]. The generalized Frobenius covariant <math display="inline">A_i</math> is evaluated by applying the polynomial to {{mvar|A}} as a matrix polynomial:
:<math display="block">A_i = f_{i,0}(A),</math>
where <math display="inline">f_{i,0}(\lambda)</math> is the degree-0 [[Hermite interpolation#Basis polynomials|Hermite interpolating basis polynomial]] corresponding to node <math display="inline">\lambda_i</math> satisfying the interpolation conditions:
:<math display="block">f_{i,0}^{(j)}(\lambda_r) = \delta_{ir}\delta_{j0} \quad (1 \le r \le k, \; 0 \le j \le m_r),</math>
where <math display="inline">\delta_{a b}</math> denotes the [[Kronecker delta]].

Let <math display="inline">f_{i,j}(\lambda)</math> denote the {{mvar|j}}-th order derivative Hermite interpolating basis polynomial corresponding to node <math display="inline">\lambda_i</math> for <math display="inline">0 \le j \le m_i</math>. In terms of the [[Jordan–Chevalley decomposition]], applying a higher-order basis polynomial <math display="inline">f_{i,j}(\lambda)</math> to matrix {{mvar|A}} isolates the {{mvar|j}}-th power of the [[nilpotent matrix]] <math display="inline">N_i = A_i (A - \lambda_i I)</math> associated with the Jordan blocks of <math display="inline">\lambda_i</math> (which is not a projection matrix for <math display="inline">j > 0</math>). When <math display="inline">j = 0</math>, the 0th power of the nilpotent matrix acts as the identity on that generalized eigenspace, reducing <math display="inline">f_{i,0}(A)</math> to the projection matrix <math display="inline">A_i</math>.

The degree-0 Hermite interpolating basis polynomial <math display="inline">f_{i,0}(\lambda)</math> can be constructed using any standard Hermite interpolation method, such as [[Hermite interpolation#Using divided differences|divided differences with confluent nodes]], [[Hermite interpolation#A perspective from linear algebra|solving a confluent Vandermonde system]], or [[Hermite interpolation#Basis polynomials via Chinese remainder theorem|via the Chinese remainder theorem]].

==== Closed-form explicit formula ====
Based on the [[Hermite interpolation#Basis polynomials in closed form|explicit formula for degree-0 Hermite interpolating basis polynomials]], define the complementary factor polynomial <math display="inline">q_i(\lambda)</math> for eigenvalue <math display="inline">\lambda_i</math> as <math display="inline">q_i(\lambda) = \prod_{r \neq i} (\lambda - \lambda_r)^{m_r + 1}</math>. The degree-0 Hermite interpolating basis polynomial <math display="inline">f_{i,0}(\lambda)</math> can be expressed directly in closed form by expanding the local Taylor polynomial:
:<math display="block">f_{i,0}(\lambda) = \left( \sum_{s=0}^{m_i} \frac{1}{s!} \left. \left( \frac{1}{q_i(z)} \right)^{(s)} \right|_{z = \lambda_i} (\lambda - \lambda_i)^s \right) q_i(\lambda).</math>

Evaluating this degree-0 Hermite interpolating basis polynomial <math display="inline">f_{i,0}(\lambda)</math> at {{mvar|A}} constructs the generalized Frobenius covariant <math display="inline">A_i = f_{i,0}(A)</math>.

=== Construction without Hermite interpolation ===
Besides constructing Hermite interpolating basis polynomials, the generalized Frobenius covariants <math display="inline">A_i</math> can also be constructed directly using several non-interpolation methods.

==== Jordan normal form ====
This approach generalizes the eigendecomposition method for distinct eigenvalues described in [[#Computing the covariants|§ Computing the covariants]] to arbitrary matrices with non-trivial Jordan blocks. If the [[Jordan normal form]] decomposition <math display="inline">A = P J P^{-1}</math> is known, <math display="inline">A_i</math> can be evaluated directly as <math display="inline">A_i = P E_i P^{-1}</math>, where <math display="inline">E_i</math> is a block diagonal matrix whose blocks corresponding to <math display="inline">\lambda_i</math> are identity matrices of matching dimensions, with all other entries set to zero.

==== Nullspace projection ====
Without finding [[Generalized eigenvector#Jordan chains|Jordan chains]], the generalized eigenspace <math display="inline">\mathcal{V}_i = \ker((A - \lambda_i I)^{m_i + 1})</math> of dimension <math display="inline">d_i = m_i + 1</math> and its complementary space <math display="inline">\mathcal{V}_i^c = \ker ( \prod_{r \neq i} (A - \lambda_r I)^{m_r + 1} )</math> of dimension <math display="inline">n - d_i</math> decompose the vector space into a direct sum <math display="inline">\mathbb{C}^n = \mathcal{V}_i \oplus \mathcal{V}_i^c</math>. In general, <math display="inline">\mathcal{V}_i</math> and <math display="inline">\mathcal{V}_i^c</math> are not orthogonal unless {{mvar|A}} is a [[normal matrix]].

Let <math display="inline">Q_{i,1} \in \mathbb{C}^{n \times d_i}</math> be a matrix whose columns form a basis for <math display="inline">\mathcal{V}_i</math>, and <math display="inline">Q_{i,2} \in \mathbb{C}^{n \times (n - d_i)}</math> be a matrix whose columns form a basis for <math display="inline">\mathcal{V}_i^c</math>. Assembling the partitioned basis matrix <math display="inline">Q_i = \begin{bmatrix} Q_{i,1} & Q_{i,2} \end{bmatrix}</math> yields
:<math display="block">A_i = Q_i \begin{bmatrix} I_{d_i} & 0 \\ 0 & 0_{n - d_i} \end{bmatrix} Q_i^{-1}.</math>

==== Holomorphic matrix functional calculus ====
Under the [[Holomorphic functional calculus#Functional calculus for a bounded operator|holomorphic matrix functional calculus]], the generalized Frobenius covariant <math display="inline">A_i</math> can be defined directly without polynomial interpolation as a [[contour integral]] of the [[resolvent formalism|resolvent matrix]] <math display="inline">(zI - A)^{-1}</math>:
:<math display="block">A_i = \frac{1}{2\pi i} \oint_{\Gamma_i} (zI - A)^{-1} \, dz,</math>
where <math display="inline">\Gamma_i</math> is a simple closed contour in the complex plane that encloses <math display="inline">\lambda_i</math> in its interior while excluding all other eigenvalues of {{mvar|A}}.
